question.title: Cloud IAM Overview
question.scenario: An administrator needs to grant a developer access to create virtual machines but not delete them.
question.question-text: What does IAM stand for and what is its purpose in GCP?

choices.choice: Identity and Access Management - controls who can do what on which resources
Internet Access Module - manages network connectivity
Infrastructure Availability Monitor - tracks resource uptime
Integrated Application Manager - deploys applications

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: IAM answers three questions for every access request: Who is making the request (identity), what action do they want to perform (permission), and on which resource? It is GCP's core access-control system.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud IAM (Identity and Access Management) is GCP's system for controlling access to resources. It defines who (identity — users, groups, service accounts) can do what (permissions grouped into roles) on which resource (scope — organization, folder, project, or individual resource). Option B fabricates a networking module that does not exist. Option C fabricates a monitoring system — uptime tracking is Cloud Monitoring's job. Option D fabricates a deployment tool. The scenario's requirement to allow VM creation but not deletion is precisely the kind of fine-grained access control IAM enables through predefined roles and custom roles.

ul.li: IAM follows the principle of least privilege — grant only the minimum permissions required for the task. For the scenario, the Compute Instance Admin (v1) role includes compute.instances.create but can be combined with deny policies to block compute.instances.delete.

IAM policies are additive by default with no implicit deny — if any policy at any level in the hierarchy grants a permission, the principal has that permission. IAM deny policies (now generally available) allow explicit denies that override allow policies.

IAM Conditions enable context-based access control, restricting permissions based on attributes like request time, source IP address, resource tags, or resource name patterns — for example, granting access only during business hours or only to resources with specific labels.

Policy inheritance flows down the resource hierarchy: a role granted at the Organization level applies to every folder, project, and resource below it. This means granting Editor at the Organization level gives broad write access everywhere — a common security mistake in GCP environments.

Policies do not inherit; each level is independent
Policies inherit downward; permissions granted at higher levels apply to lower levels
Policies only inherit within the same region

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: IAM policies flow downward through the resource hierarchy — a role granted at the Organization or folder level automatically applies to every project and resource contained within it, no per-project configuration needed.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: IAM policies inherit downward through the resource hierarchy: Organization to Folder to Project to Resource. A role granted at a higher level automatically applies to all lower-level resources. In the scenario, granting Storage Admin at the folder level means the user has Storage Admin in every project within that folder. Option A reverses the direction — policies never flow upward. Option B is wrong because inheritance is fundamental to GCP IAM. Option D is incorrect because IAM inheritance follows the resource hierarchy, not geographic regions. Policies are additive: lower levels can add permissions but cannot remove inherited permissions without deny policies.

ul.li: The effective policy on any resource is the union of all inherited policies from above plus any policies set directly on that resource — this means a user can accumulate permissions from Organization, folder, project, and resource-level bindings simultaneously.

Prior to IAM deny policies, you could not revoke inherited permissions at lower levels — if someone was granted Editor at the Organization, they had Editor everywhere. IAM deny policies now allow explicit permission denials that override allow policies at any level.

Best practice is to grant roles at the narrowest scope needed for the task — if a user only needs Storage Admin in one project, grant it at the project level rather than the folder level to avoid unintended access to other projects in the same folder.

IAM Policy Analyzer lets you query "who has access to what" across the hierarchy by evaluating all allow and deny policies, including inherited ones — essential for security audits and compliance reviews where you need to prove access is appropriately scoped.

question.title: Service Account Keys
question.scenario: A developer wants to run GCP commands from their local machine and is considering downloading a service account key file.
question.question-text: What is the security best practice regarding service account keys?

choices.choice: Store key files in source code repositories
Avoid key files; use attached service accounts, Workload Identity, or gcloud authentication instead
Share key files among team members for convenience
Download keys for all service accounts for backup purposes

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Service account key files are long-lived credentials that pose significant security risks if leaked or stolen. Best practice is to avoid creating them entirely and use safer alternatives like attached service accounts or gcloud auth.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Service account key files are downloadable JSON credentials that never expire unless explicitly deleted, making them a persistent security risk. Best practice is to avoid them entirely. For GCP-hosted workloads, use attached service accounts. For GKE, use Workload Identity. For local development, use gcloud auth application-default login. Option A is one of the worst practices — committing keys to source control is a leading cause of cloud security breaches. Option C destroys individual accountability since all users share one identity. Option D creates unnecessary credentials that expand the attack surface without benefit.

ul.li: Service account key files never expire on their own — they remain valid indefinitely unless explicitly deleted or the service account itself is disabled, which means a leaked key can provide persistent unauthorized access until discovered and revoked.

Organization policies can disable service account key creation entirely using the iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation constraint, preventing any project in the organization from generating new key files — a strong guardrail for security-conscious enterprises.

Cloud Audit Logs track service account key usage including which key was used, from which IP address, and for which API call — enabling security teams to detect anomalous usage patterns that might indicate a compromised key.

For local development, gcloud auth application-default login provides short-lived, automatically refreshed credentials that follow your user identity, offering the same convenience as key files without the persistent credential risk. For CI/CD pipelines, Workload Identity Federation from GitHub Actions, GitLab, or Jenkins eliminates keys entirely.

question.title: Committed Use Discounts
question.scenario: A company has predictable compute workloads running 24/7 and wants to reduce costs.
question.question-text: What are Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) in GCP?

choices.choice: Automatic discounts applied to all resources
Discounts for committing to use specific resources for 1 or 3 years
Discounts for using resources only during off-peak hours
Discounts for using deprecated services

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: CUDs provide significant discounts — up to 57% for 3-year terms — in exchange for committing to a minimum level of resource usage over a 1-year or 3-year period, regardless of whether you use the full committed amount.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) offer significant savings in exchange for committing to use specific amounts of compute resources for 1-year (up to 37% discount) or 3-year terms (up to 57% discount). Option A is wrong — CUDs require an explicit commitment and are not automatic (Sustained Use Discounts are automatic). Option C fabricates an off-peak pricing model that does not exist in GCP. Option D fabricates a deprecation discount that does not exist. CUDs are ideal for the scenario's predictable 24/7 workloads because the steady usage guarantees the committed resources will be fully utilized, maximizing savings.

ul.li: GCP offers two types of CUDs: resource-based CUDs where you commit to specific amounts of vCPU and memory in a region (applied automatically to eligible VMs), and spend-based CUDs where you commit to a dollar amount of spending on specific services like Cloud SQL or Cloud Run.

Resource-based CUDs apply automatically to eligible usage in the committed region — you do not need to assign specific VMs to a commitment. If you commit to 16 vCPUs in us-central1, any combination of VMs using those vCPUs receives the discounted rate.

CUDs cannot be canceled once purchased — you are charged for the committed amount monthly for the entire term even if your actual usage drops below the commitment level. Careful capacity planning is essential before purchasing CUDs.

CUDs and Sustained Use Discounts do not stack — GCP applies the better discount. For workloads running 24/7, a 3-year CUD provides up to 57% savings compared to the 30% maximum from Sustained Use Discounts alone, making CUDs the better choice for predictable long-running workloads.

question.title: Sustained Use Discounts
question.scenario: A company runs Compute Engine instances continuously throughout the month without any special commitments.
question.question-text: What are Sustained Use Discounts in GCP?

choices.choice: Automatic discounts for resources running more than 25% of the month
Discounts requiring a 3-year commitment
Discounts for using preemptible VMs
Discounts for new GCP customers only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Sustained Use Discounts are automatic price reductions that kick in when you run Compute Engine resources for a significant portion of the month, increasing as usage increases — no commitment or action required from you.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs) are automatic discounts that GCP applies when Compute Engine resources run for a significant portion of the billing month. Discounts increase incrementally as usage grows, reaching up to 30% off for resources running the entire month. Option B describes Committed Use Discounts, which require an explicit commitment. Option C describes the discount model for Spot/Preemptible VMs, which is a separate mechanism. Option D is wrong — SUDs apply to all customers, not just new ones. The key advantage is that SUDs require no action, commitment, or configuration — they appear automatically on your bill.

ul.li: SUDs are calculated in four incremental tiers based on monthly usage: 0-25% at full price, 25-50% at a reduced rate, 50-75% at a further reduced rate, and 75-100% at the lowest rate — the blended effective discount reaches approximately 30% for resources running all month.

GCP aggregates usage of the same machine type within a region across all VMs for SUD calculation — so running two n1-standard-4 VMs for half the month each is equivalent to running one for the full month, and both receive the combined sustained discount.

SUDs apply to vCPU and memory charges for N1, N2, and N2D general-purpose machine types, but notably do not apply to E2 machine types or to resources already covered by Committed Use Discounts — E2 instances are already priced lower as a cost-optimized family.

For workloads that run continuously, Committed Use Discounts provide larger savings than SUDs (up to 57% vs 30%), but SUDs serve as a no-commitment safety net for usage patterns that are not predictable enough to justify a commitment purchase.

question.title: Preemptible and Spot VMs
question.scenario: A company runs batch processing jobs that can tolerate interruptions and restart if needed.
question.question-text: What is the benefit of using Spot VMs (formerly Preemptible VMs) in GCP?

choices.choice: Up to 91% cost savings, but instances can be terminated with 30-second notice
Guaranteed uptime with premium support included
Free usage with no time limits
Priority scheduling over regular VMs

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Spot VMs use GCP's excess compute capacity at steep discounts of 60-91% off standard pricing, but the trade-off is that GCP can reclaim them at any time with only 30 seconds notice when capacity is needed for regular workloads.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Spot VMs offer 60-91% discounts compared to regular on-demand pricing by utilizing GCP's excess compute capacity. The trade-off is that GCP can terminate them with only 30 seconds notice when it needs the capacity back. Option B is the opposite of reality — Spot VMs have no uptime guarantee and no SLA. Option C is wrong because Spot VMs are not free, just heavily discounted. Option D is backwards — Spot VMs have lower scheduling priority than regular VMs. The scenario's fault-tolerant batch processing jobs are ideal because they can checkpoint progress and restart from where they left off after preemption.

ul.li: Spot VMs replaced the older Preemptible VM model — the key difference is that Preemptible VMs had a hard 24-hour maximum runtime limit and were always terminated after 24 hours, while Spot VMs have no such time limit and run until preempted by capacity demands or stopped by the user.

Spot VMs have no SLA for availability and can be preempted at any time, making them unsuitable for user-facing production services, but perfect for batch processing, CI/CD pipelines, rendering jobs, scientific simulations, and any workload that can be interrupted and restarted.

Managed instance groups with Spot VMs automatically recreate instances after preemption, providing a self-healing compute pool — combined with checkpointing application state to Cloud Storage, this enables reliable batch processing at a fraction of on-demand cost.

You can mix Spot and regular VMs in the same managed instance group to balance cost savings with availability — for example, maintaining a baseline of regular VMs for steady work while adding Spot VMs for burst capacity during peak processing periods.

question.question-text: What is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) in GCP?

choices.choice: A software-defined network providing connectivity for GCP resources
A physical datacenter dedicated to one customer
A type of virtual machine
A storage bucket with private access

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A VPC is a software-defined virtual network that provides isolated connectivity for your GCP resources. You control IP address ranges, subnets, routes, and firewall rules within it, similar to a traditional on-premises network but in the cloud.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A VPC is a global, software-defined network that provides connectivity, isolation, and security for GCP resources like Compute Engine VMs, GKE clusters, and Cloud SQL instances. You define IP ranges, create subnets, configure routes, and set firewall rules. Option B confuses VPC with a dedicated physical datacenter, which would be Bare Metal Solution or a colocation arrangement. Option C confuses VPC with a VM, which is a compute resource that connects to a VPC. Option D confuses VPC with a Cloud Storage bucket, which is an object storage resource. VPCs are global in scope but contain regional subnets, providing a flexible networking layer that spans GCP's infrastructure.

ul.li: GCP VPCs are global resources, meaning a single VPC can contain subnets in different regions around the world — this is unique to GCP and different from AWS and Azure where virtual networks are regional, simplifying multi-region architectures.

Auto mode VPCs create one subnet per region automatically with predefined IP ranges, suitable for simple setups. Custom mode VPCs give you full control over subnet creation, IP addressing, and region selection — custom mode is recommended for production environments.

VPC peering connects two VPCs for private communication without going through the public internet, and Shared VPC allows a host project to share its VPC subnets with service projects — enabling centralized network management while letting teams deploy resources in their own projects.

Private Google Access allows VM instances without external IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, etc.) through internal routing, eliminating the need for NAT gateways or external IPs just to access GCP services.

hint.content: GCP provides multiple support tiers: Basic (free, self-service documentation and community forums), Standard (paid, business-hours technical support), Enhanced (paid, 24/7 support for critical issues with faster response times), and Premium (paid, fastest response with a dedicated Technical Account Manager).
